case_name: Mushtak Hussein v State of Bombay
respondent:
State of Bombay
Supreme Court of India

30 March 1953
Criminal Appeal No.96 of
1952
The Judgment was delivered by : Mehr Chand Mahajan, J.
1. The appellant on 28th July, 1951, was convicted on a charge under section 366, Indian Penal Code, for having kidnapped at Poona a minor girl Shilavati in order that she may be forced or seduced to illicit intercourse and was sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for two years after a trial before the third additional Sessions Judge of that place sitting with a jury of live. The jury returned a verdict of guilty by a majority of three to two. The Sessions Judge came to the conclusion that the verdict was not perverse. He therefore accepted it. The appellant preferred an appeal to the High Court but this was summarily dismissed. This appeal is before us by special leave.

facts: The appellant was convicted on a charge under section 366, Indian Penal Code, for having kidnapped a minor girl Shilavati in order that she may be forced or seduced to illicit intercourse.
The prosecution case was that the appellant, who was a music teacher, went to Shilavati's house and took her to his house with the assistance of one Iqbal Putlabai (accused 2).
Shilavati was traced in Bombay after four months in the house of one Babu Konde. Thereafter she was medically examined and it was found that she was pregnant.

Yamunabai, the mother of Shilavati, stated that on 12th December when she returned home in the evening she learnt from her sister-in-law Jamunabai and others that the appellant had taken Shilavati on the pretext that he wanted to compare her voice with that of one Prabha who was waiting in his house.
Ananda, uncle of the girl, deposed to the same effect.
Prahlad, brother of Shilavati, a boy of school-going age, deposed that he saw Shilavati going with the appellant while he was playing outside the school.
Namdeo, who is a bricklayer, stated that on the 12th December while he was returning after completing his work at about 3-30 p.m. he saw Shilavati going with the appellant.
issues: Whether the judge misdirected the jury in several important particulars and violated the rules of criminal jurisprudence and of evidence in a number of ways.
Whether the jury's verdict was perverse or not.
petitioner_arguments: The learned counsel for the appellant contended that the judge in his charge to the jury misdirected it in several important particulars and violated the rules of criminal jurisprudence and of evidence in a number of ways.
It was said that he failed to warn the jury that it would be unsafe for it to act on the statement of Shilavati without her statement being corroborated by other evidence, in material particulars.
respondent_arguments: The prosecution examined in all sixteen witnesses. Out of these four were eye-witnesses, viz., Prahlad, Jamunabai, Namdeo and Shilavati.

Yamunabai, the mother of Shilavati, stated that on 12th December when she returned home in the evening she learnt from her sister-in-law Jamunabai and others that the appellant had taken Shilavati on the pretext that he wanted to compare her voice with that of one Prabha who was waiting in his house.
court_reasoning: In our judgment, it is not necessary to pronounce on all the points urged by the learned counsel, because we are of the opinion that the judge clearly misdirected the jury when he asked it to solve the problem that had arisen by exercising its ingenuity and by resorting, if necessary, to speculative reasoning.
holding: The appeal is allowed. The conviction and sentence are set aside.
